extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics researchers (especially early-career researchers and students)
extracted.subtask_description: Short career/advice guidance for doing mathematical research: how to approach problems, manage expectations, and choose strategies (patience, deferral, skill-building, and scepticism about easy breakthroughs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient attention / patience
rubrics_metrics.description: If I have ever made any valuable discoveries, it has been owing more to patient attention, than to any other talent. Any given problem generally requires months of effort... Thus it is not uncommon for months to pass with no visible progress; however by patiently eliminating fruitless avenues of attack, you are setting things up so that when the breakthrough does come, one can conclude the problem in relatively short order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat problem-solving as a long-term process: expect to invest months (rather than days or weeks) and repeatedly prune unproductive approaches. Persistence and careful, patient work (eliminating fruitless avenues) are the primary drivers of eventual success. See also the author's linked posts 'work hard' and 'be flexible' for complementary advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations about 'Eureka' moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Most problems are solved primarily by this sort of patient, thoughtful attack; there are remarkably few 'Eureka!' moments in this business, and don’t be discouraged if they don’t magically appear for you (they certainly don’t for me).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on or expect sudden flashes of insight as the norm. Mental resilience is required: lack of dramatic breakthroughs is normal and not an indicator of personal failure. Cultivate steady, methodical work habits instead of waiting for inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic deferral and skill-building
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, you (or the mathematical field in general) are simply not ready to tackle the problem yet; in this case, setting it aside (but not forgetting it entirely), building up some skill on other related problems, and returning back to the original problem in a couple years is often the optimal strategy (particularly if your formal mathematical education is still not complete). This is particularly likely to be the case for any really famous problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When progress stalls because of lack of background or techniques, intentionally defer the problem and work on related problems to acquire necessary skills and perspective. Keep the problem in mind (don’t forget it entirely) so you can return later; for famous or deep problems, multi-year postponement plus focused skill acquisition is often optimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of breakthroughs that seem 'too easy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of any breakthrough which was 'too easy' and mysteriously failed to address the key difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating purported solutions or personal sudden insights, critically check whether the proposed approach truly addresses the core difficulty rather than hiding or bypassing it. Treat unusually easy-sounding solutions with caution and verify they handle the central obstacles.
